MonitoringApproach:
The base impervious coverage layer for the Region was sourced from a LiDAR

survey completed in August 2010. LiDAR is a remote sensing technology that uses laser and light refraction to image objects and terrain. The 2010 LiDAR analysis mapped the extent of hard and soft

impervious cover in the Region. The cost of acquiring LiDAR data for the Region makes quadrennial LiDAR surveys infeasible. To assess change in impervious cover without the benefit of new LiDAR imagery, information collected from project permitting by TRPA and partners was used to determine added/new coverage. Land capability as defined in the 2007 soil survey was used as the primary unit to measure coverage in a land capability class, both because it was used in the 2011 Threshold Evaluation Report (TRPA, 2012b) and because it is more detailed than the 1974 Bailey report (Loftis, 2007). Information about coverage removed was provided by the CTC, NDSL and the Parcel Tracker.

measures.sub: Acres of impervious coverage in each land capability district and the coverage the district allows, 2023 Threshold Evaluation.

measures.title: Impervious surface, 2019
measures.sub: Acres of mapped impervious surface by type, hard and soft surfaces.

measures.title: Impervious surface, 2010
measures.sub: Acres of mapped impervious surface by type, hard and soft surfaces, from the 2010 LiDAR mapping.

measures.title: Coverage change, 2010 to 2019
measures.sub: Acres of impervious coverage added, removed, or changed in type between the two mappings. Mapping corrections are left out.
measures.where: General_Status IN ('New Coverage','Removed Coverage','Changed Coverage Type')

measures.title: Land capability district acres
measures.sub: Acres in each Bailey (1974) land capability district, from 1A (most sensitive) to 7.

measures.title: Coverage allowed by district
measures.sub: Acres of impervious coverage the Bailey coefficients allow in each district: 1 percent in districts 1 and 2, up to 30 percent in districts 6 and 7.
